## Before you upgrade

- **OpenSearch's own audit log is on.** The Docker quick start, the Helm chart and new installs turn on OpenSearch's audit log, without request bodies or passwords. On an OpenSearch you set up yourself, first load Signalith's `audit.yml` with `securityadmin.sh -f audit.yml -t audit`, then change `plugins.security.audit.type` to `log4j` and restart OpenSearch. See [OpenSearch's own audit log](https://signalith.io/docs/opensearch-security/#opensearchs-own-audit-log).
- **Shards are automatic.** When `opensearch.shards` is not set, each new day's events get one primary shard per OpenSearch data node (up to 8) instead of one, and a busy day rolls over to a new index (`...-2026.10.17-2`) at 40 GB per shard (`opensearch.rollover_gb`). On a single OpenSearch node nothing changes. To keep one shard on a larger cluster, set `opensearch.shards: 1`. See [Server settings](https://signalith.io/docs/settings/#using-the-page).
- **Spread primary shards on an OpenSearch of several nodes.** Add `cluster.routing.allocation.balance.prefer_primary: true` and `cluster.routing.allocation.rebalance.primary.enable: true` to each node's `opensearch.yml` (or set them once with `PUT _cluster/settings`). Without the first OpenSearch may put every primary of a busy day on one node, which then does nearly all the indexing; without the second, a node's primaries stay on the others after it restarts. The three-node Docker quick start and the Helm chart set it, and the Servers page warns when today's primaries share one node. See [OpenSearch with several nodes](https://signalith.io/docs/opensearch-failover/#what-you-need).
- **Detections spread over servers by default.** With two or more servers that may run the background jobs, each runs a share of the rules (`detections.spread` is now on unless you turned it off). A single server runs every rule as before. In a 3-server lab test each server took about a third of the rules, with no late runs through a restart and a crash. To keep every rule on one server, turn off **Spread detections over servers** under Settings > Detections. See [Servers](https://signalith.io/docs/servers/).
- **New installs name the built-in admin `signalithadmin`.** `admin` is the first name password-guessing attacks try, so new installs (`signalith init`, the packages, the Docker quick start and the Helm chart) use `signalithadmin` instead. An existing install keeps the name it has and signs in as before: package and Windows installs keep their `signalith.yaml`, and Docker and Helm installs keep the name their servers share. One exception: a Docker or Helm install still on 0.1.0 has no shared users yet, so after this upgrade its built-in admin is `signalithadmin`, with the same password. To keep `admin` there, set `auth.admin_user: admin` before upgrading. See [Users](https://signalith.io/docs/users/#the-built-in-admin).
- **`min(_time)` and `max(_time)` are in seconds.** Stats over `_time` (`min`, `max`, `avg`, `range` and the like) now give seconds since 1970, as Splunk does, where they gave milliseconds (or nothing, after a command that runs in Signalith). A saved search or dashboard that divided them by 1000 should stop doing so. Findings stored before the upgrade keep the milliseconds their rules wrote in fields such as `first_seen` and `last_seen`. See [Query language](https://signalith.io/docs/query-language/).
- **`stdev` and `var` of a single value are 0, and `_time` is a number in expressions.** As in Splunk, `stdev(x)` over one value gives 0 instead of nothing, so a check like `x >= avg + 3*stdev` now holds for a group of one; and `where`, `eval` and search terms such as `_time>=1767268800` read `_time` as seconds since 1970 (a number in a search term was read as milliseconds before). See [Query language](https://signalith.io/docs/query-language/#expressions-eval-and-where).
- **The Windows installer sets up OpenSearch.** A new install from the `.msi` (or `install.ps1`) downloads OpenSearch 3.9.0 for Windows, checks it against the SHA-512 Signalith pins, and runs it as the SignalithOpenSearch service on this computer only, over HTTPS, with Signalith signing in with a certificate. An existing install keeps the OpenSearch it uses. To use your own OpenSearch on a new install, give `OPENSEARCHURL`; without internet access, give the release's .zip with `OPENSEARCHZIP`. See [OpenSearch on Windows](https://signalith.io/docs/install-packages/#opensearch-on-windows).
- **New installs take syslog over TLS only.** Plain syslog over UDP and TCP 514 is unencrypted and anyone who can reach the port can send fake events, so `signalith init`, the packages, the Windows installer, the Docker quick start and the Helm chart now turn on syslog over TLS (port 6514) only on a new install. For devices that can only send plain syslog, an admin turns it on with one click: **Turn on plain syslog (UDP and TCP)** on **Add data** > **Syslog**, then **Restart now**. **Upgrades keep plain syslog as it was:** package, Windows and hand-made installs keep their `signalith.yaml`; a Docker quick start set up before keeps UDP and TCP on 514, decided once at its first start with this version (noted in `plain-syslog.json` in the `signalith-data` volume); and a Helm upgrade keeps it when the release's syslog Service takes port 514 (`server.syslog.plain` is `auto`; `true` or `false` decides). Tools that render the chart without a cluster (`helm template`, Argo CD, Flux) can't see the old Service, so if you deploy that way and devices send to 514, set `server.syslog.plain: true`. Turning plain syslog on or off on the Settings page now asks for your password again. Turn it off on the Settings page once every device sends over TLS. See [Turning on plain syslog](https://signalith.io/docs/sending-data/#turning-on-plain-syslog).
- **Windows: an install that never reached OpenSearch gets one on upgrade.** If your 0.3.0 install never connected to OpenSearch (it still has the default `http://127.0.0.1:9200` and nothing answers there), the 0.3.1 installer sets up OpenSearch for you on upgrade, on port 9201 or the next free one, and keeps your old configuration as `signalith.yaml.before-opensearch`. An OpenSearch you configured yourself is left as it is. Reinstalling after deleting `C:\ProgramData\Signalith` while OpenSearch's own folder is kept also works now.

## What's new

**Signalith Agent**
- One install line per computer for Linux, Windows and macOS, under **Add data** > **Signalith Agent**. It runs Fluent Bit and osquery, with optional Sysmon on Windows. Choose what each install line collects on the Endpoints page. See [Signalith Agent](https://signalith.io/docs/signalith-agent/).
- Agents update themselves to later releases, checked against a signed list of agent programs, and roll back if the new one fails. This is the first release signed with the agent release key. Turn **Automatic updates** off for an install line to hold its computers at their version.

**Getting started**
- An optional setup guide walks a new admin through the first steps after signing in.
- The Windows installer sets up OpenSearch on the same computer (see above), so one `.msi` gives a working server.
- **Add data** explains why to pick the Signalith Agent and shows each source's steps right below it.
- A public, read-only [demo mode](https://signalith.io/docs/demo/): visitors see every analyst page filled with sample data, and a cloud-init file sets up a demo server. Try it at [demo.signalith.io](https://demo.signalith.io).

**Search and investigation**
- Click an event to see all its fields. Side panels can be widened or opened to the full page.
- An [attack storyline](https://signalith.io/docs/storyline/) shows the findings of one intrusion as a single story: when it started, which ATT&CK tactics it reached in what order, and which accounts, systems and processes tie it together.
- More SPL: `union`, `geostats`, `extract`, `outlier`, `gauge`, `multisearch`, `timewrap`, `cluster`, `xpath`, `abstract`, `highlight`, `anomalydetection`, `correlate`, `predict`, `set`, `setfields`, `kmeans`, `eventcount`, `outputlookup` and `from`, lookup tables with wildcard and ignore-case matching, subsearches among search terms, and many smaller syntax forms. `iplocation` fills the same fields as Splunk's.
- A search reads only the days in its time range.
- `timechart ... by` picks its series over the whole range and counts each in every bucket, where a value outside one bucket's top 10 showed 0 there; it adds `OTHER` and `NULL` series as Splunk does (`useother=f`, `usenull=f` leave them out).
- Closer to Splunk: `sort 10 -count` keeps 10 rows and sort keys take `num()`, `str()`, `ip()` and `auto()`; a multivalue field matches `where` and `search` when one of its values does; `stats` and `top` by a multivalue field count each value; `values()` keeps up to 10,000 values with their types and marks the result truncated when it leaves some out.
- `stats sum(bytes*)` and `stats values(*) as *` cover every matching field, as in Splunk, where the pattern was read as one field's name and gave nothing; `timechart`, `chart`, `streamstats` and `by *` refuse a `*` field name instead of returning empty columns. New: `head limit=N`, `stdevp`, `varp` and `sumsq`, and the eval functions `sha512`, `random`, `pi`, `exact`, `isbool`, `ipmask`, `atan2`, `hypot` and the trigonometric functions.
- The Search page runs searches in your browser's time zone, shown next to the results: `@d` and the other snaps, `timechart` and `bin` days and weeks, `strftime` and `relative_time` follow it instead of UTC. Detections and dashboards still run in UTC.
- A result is marked **Sampled** when commands such as `eval`, `rename`, `bin` or `dedup` before `stats` ran over only the newest `search.max_events` events of more that matched, so its counts cover only those; Explain says so too. Backtests count such runs as capped.
- With more than 50,000 groups, `top`, `rare` and `stats ... | sort -count | head N` keep the largest groups (ranked in OpenSearch) instead of the first 50,000 by name, so the top rows are the right ones; such results show **Ranked**.
- On the Risk page, each entry under *What added risk* opens the detection that added the risk, with links to the finding raised with it (or the risk event in Search, for a risk-only detection). The ATT&CK tactic chips filter the list to one tactic.
- **Ask** points to AI setup and names the local model option (Ollama).

**Data and detections**
- An [intake for Splunk HEC senders](https://signalith.io/docs/hec/), so tools built for Splunk's HTTP Event Collector can send to Signalith.
- 1,330 rules from Splunk Security Content and 2,638 from SigmaHQ, each tested on sample events. New: macOS process starts, PowerShell module logging and the Windows PowerShell log, the System, WMI, AppX and Application logs, and Splunk's lookup tables.
- Industrial protocols from the network sensor go to a new **Industrial** data model: Modbus and DNP3 from Zeek, S7comm, EtherNet/IP and CIP, BACnet, OPC UA, PROFINET and more from CISA's free ICSNPP analyzers, and Suricata's Modbus, DNP3 and EtherNet/IP events, each with one function name and kind (read, write, control, program) whichever tool saw it. Nothing changes on networks without them. See [Industrial protocols](https://signalith.io/docs/network-sensor/#industrial-protocols).
- Seven industrial detections (controller stop or restart, program upload or download, commands from outside, device discovery, error bursts, Modbus listen-only, and a new command source, off by default), mapped to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS with a second matrix on the Coverage page, an **Industrial network** dashboard, and two sample stories that show them firing. See [Industrial detections](https://signalith.io/docs/detections/#industrial-detections).
- A detection that needs a GeoIP database shows **Needs setup** on a server without one, instead of a query error.
- Microsoft Defender events can also come through the OpenTelemetry Collector on Windows (Collector 0.129 or later). The Symantec, ClamAV, ESET PROTECT, CrowdStrike, Kaspersky and Trellix ePO parsers are now tested against real published logs, with the gaps those logs showed fixed. See [Antivirus](https://signalith.io/docs/antivirus/).
- Credentialed OpenVAS scans can also sign in to VMware ESXi hosts and to network devices over SNMP.
- Each tenant has its own behavior baselines.

**Backup and restore**
- `signalith backup` and `signalith restore` save and bring back one server's own files: its settings, detections, dashboards, lists and keys. The master key goes in a separate `<backup>.master-key.zip` by default, so the two can be stored apart (`-include-master-key` and `-no-master-key` change that, and `restore -master-key` takes it back). Backup files are private to the account that made them, on Windows too. The Docker quick start adds a volume for OpenSearch snapshots and a `snapshot.sh` script. See [Backup and restore](https://signalith.io/docs/backup/).

**Several servers and large installs**
- Detections spread over servers by default (see above). The Servers page shows detection health and how many detection groups each server runs.
- Index shards are sized from the OpenSearch data nodes, busy days roll over to a new index, and primaries move back after an OpenSearch node restarts.
- Tested at about 21,500 events a second on one server, and at 25,000 events a second on three servers with 1,520 detections, with no late detections. See [Performance](https://signalith.io/docs/performance/).
- Servers never rejoin with a cluster key that a rotation retired.

**Security**
- New installs use `signalithadmin` as the built-in admin and take syslog over TLS only (see above).
- OpenSearch's own audit log is on.
- Every search is audited: who ran it, from where, the query, its time range and indices, and how it ended, for searches, dashboards, panel previews, notebooks and investigations. Pick **Searches** on the Audit page. See [Audit](https://signalith.io/docs/audit/#searches).
- Compliance: NIS2 and GDPR added. NIS2 covers the Article 21 measures a SIEM can show and the Article 23 reporting deadlines (24 hours, 72 hours, one month); the GDPR covers how Signalith treats the personal data in your logs, security of processing and breach notification. Both say plainly that a SIEM gives evidence but does not make you compliant. See [Compliance](https://signalith.io/docs/compliance/#nis2-and-the-gdpr).
- A [threat model](https://signalith.io/docs/threat-model/), and governance, architecture and code review docs. Signalith has the OpenSSF Best Practices silver badge.
- Every source file carries a copyright and SPDX license line.
